candidates.lesson_subject: Dynamic BGP learning of FortiGuard ISDB botnet and spam reputation IPs
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: BGP network statements reference FortiGuard Internet Service Database reputation categories Botnet-C&C.Server and Spam-Spamming.Server; FortiGate dynamically learns and advertises reputation IP prefixes through BGP rather than relying only on static prefix lists.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: ISDB reputation feed -> FortiGate BGP network item using internet-service-name -> BGP UPDATE to authorized peers -> downstream route policy/sinkhole/blackhole decision; route advertisement is separate from local firewall blocking.
candidates.failure_class: Threat-intelligence route export missing, stale, overbroad, or rejected by BGP policy.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Peer BGP RIB shows dynamic /32 routes; local ISDB query shows category membership; received/advertised route and route-map counters prove propagation, not that data-plane traffic is blocked.
candidates.remediation_path: Verify FortiGuard/ISDB entitlement and category name, BGP network statement, peer activation and outbound route-map, prefix acceptance, next-hop reachability, and downstream discard/sinkhole policy.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Distinguish ISDB-driven BGP prefix origination from static networks, redistribution, and local firewall deny.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Threat-feed-to-FortiGate-ISDB-to-BGP-originator-to-two-peers topology with a separate downstream enforcement branch.
candidates.uniqueness_rationale: No in-window FortiGate lesson covers dynamic BGP origination from ISDB reputation categories. Prior BGP lessons concern route maps, transport, route leaking, TCP-AO, conditional advertisement, and route-reflector next-hop; prior SD-WAN IPAM/route-tag items use different mechanisms.

candidates.lesson_subject: Dynamic MAC learning limits, violation shutdown, aging and sticky MAC persistence
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Per-port or per-VLAN dynamic source-MAC learning can be limited; learned entries age out; sticky MAC preserves learned identities across port link transitions and can be saved for reboot; violation logging and timed shutdown are separate controls.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Frame source MAC arrives -> switch learns dynamic FDB entry if learning enabled -> limit evaluated -> violation action/log controlled globally and per interface -> aging or sticky persistence determines entry lifetime.
candidates.failure_class: MAC learning limit exceeded without shutdown or event evidence because violation timer/logging are disabled, or stale sticky entries block legitimate endpoint moves.
candidates.evidence_pattern: MAC limit violation table, physical port state, system log, MAC event log, FDB entry and sticky-save state; static MACs are not counted in dynamic limit.
candidates.remediation_path: Set a non-zero mac-violation-timer, enable log-mac-limit-violations, configure per-port learning-limit/action, verify port state and violation table, reset violation state after remediation, and persist sticky entries only when required.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Diagnose why learning-limit-action shutdown did not shut a port and distinguish the global timer/logging prerequisites from the per-port threshold.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Access switch port with endpoint MACs feeding dynamic FDB and limit counter, with separate violation-log/timer/shutdown branch and sticky-MAC persistence store.
candidates.uniqueness_rationale: No prior lesson covers dynamic MAC FDB admission, learning-limit violation lifecycle, or sticky MAC persistence. Prior switch lessons cover IP source guard, DHCP snooping, MAB, MACsec, LACP, STP, VXLAN and port policies.

candidates.lesson_subject: Audit-only compliance scans versus Forced Remediation Exceptions
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiNAC separates compliance evaluation from enforcement using scan-level Audit Only and host-group-level Forced Remediation Exceptions; Audit Only prevents failed hosts from being marked at-risk, while exception-group members may be marked at-risk but are never forced into Remediation.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Policy assignment selects scan -> scan evaluates host and stores result -> Audit Only or exception-group membership determines remediation transition -> quarantine/remediation switching is bypassed for selected scope.
candidates.failure_class: A compliance test unexpectedly interrupts users, or a noncompliant endpoint remains connected because enforcement suppression scope was misunderstood.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Scan definition Audit Only flag, host group membership, stored scan result, host at-risk state and remediation state; result storage does not imply enforcement.
candidates.remediation_path: Choose scan-level Audit Only for one scan's evaluated population or exception-group membership for hosts across scans; preserve other enforcing scans; validate with test hosts and inspect both result and remediation state.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Identify the difference between scan-scoped non-enforcement and host-group-scoped remediation exception semantics.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Host enters assigned scan; result branch marks compliant/noncompliant; separate Audit Only and exception-group gates converge on remain-connected versus remediation VLAN.
candidates.uniqueness_rationale: Historical FortiNAC lessons cover scans, profiling, policy assignment, host timers, and authentication, but none covers decoupling scan result storage from remediation enforcement.

candidates.lesson_subject: OAuth authorization-code flow with PKCE for public relying parties
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Public OAuth relying parties use Authorization Code with PKCE; client_secret is ignored at authorize, S256 code_challenge/code_challenge_method are required, and token exchange requires code_verifier matching the issued challenge.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Public client generates verifier -> derives S256 challenge -> /oauth/authorize redirects user to FortiAuthenticator portal and issues code -> client sends code plus verifier to /oauth/token -> FAC validates SHA256 relationship before issuing token.
candidates.failure_class: Authorization-code interception or token exchange failure from missing/mismatched PKCE parameters, wrong redirect URI, or using confidential-client assumptions with a public client.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Relying-party client type/grant type, authorize request parameters, token request code_verifier, redirect URI and FAC OAuth error/response; a successful login alone does not prove correct token binding.
candidates.remediation_path: Set client type Public and grant Authorization code with PKCE, use S256 only, preserve verifier securely for the exchange, register exact HTTPS redirect URI, and verify token request challenge match.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Identify which PKCE fields belong in authorize versus token exchange and what happens to client_secret for a public client.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Public app with verifier/challenge branch, browser redirect to FAC login, authorization code return, token endpoint verifier validation, access-token output.
candidates.uniqueness_rationale: Prior FortiAuthenticator lessons cover SAML, RADIUS, TACACS+, LDAP and certificate revocation; no prior lesson covers OAuth PKCE or the public-client verifier binding.

candidates.lesson_subject: Kerberos authentication for native RDP Network Level Authentication
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiPAM 1.9 native RDP launcher can use Kerberos for NLA/CredSSP; realm derives from secret/target domain, KDC is selected by explicit KDC Address or DNS SRV discovery, and feature is limited to native RDP launcher.

candidates.failure_class: RDP NLA falls back to NTLM or fails Kerberos due missing FQDN/domain association, KDC discovery, SPN, DNS or time prerequisites.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Secret RDP Security Level=NLA and Use Kerberos for NLA, target domain/FQDN/KDC Address, DNS SRV resolution and native launcher behavior; Web RDP is not supported for this option.
candidates.remediation_path: Use native RDP, configure NLA and Kerberos, associate a Windows Domain Account secret with Target Only FQDN secret or enter target FQDN, verify realm/KDC discovery, and use explicit KDC Address only when needed.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Select the valid FortiPAM RDP Kerberos path and distinguish it from TCP forwarding, Web RDP and NTLM NLA.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiPAM secret and target feed realm/FQDN, KDC discovery (DNS SRV or explicit address), Kerberos ticket, then native RDP NLA session.
candidates.uniqueness_rationale: No prior FortiPAM lesson covers Kerberos ticket acquisition for native RDP NLA. Prior RDP lessons cover TCP forwarding, launchers, clipboard/security controls, but not Kerberos realm/KDC selection.

candidates.lesson_subject: Endpoint-to-endpoint communication through Secure Private Access hubs
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiSASE allows remote endpoints on Cloud Security tunnels to communicate through an SPA Hub; BGP endpoint-to-endpoint traffic is enabled, hub re-announces Security PoP prefixes, and policy requirements differ for same versus different Security PoPs.

candidates.remediation_path: Configure at least one SPA Hub, enable Endpoint-to-endpoint Traffic, re-announce Security PoP prefixes on hubs, add same-PoP endpoint-to-endpoint policies or cross-PoP To/From Hub policies, and log denied traffic.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Choose the required policy and BGP action for same-PoP versus cross-PoP endpoint communication.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Two remote endpoints behind separate Security PoPs connected through SPA Hub, BGP prefix exchange, with same-PoP endpoint policy and cross-PoP To/From Hub policy branches.
